The State Must Ban Virtual Simulated Crimes Because Experience, Technology, and Core Liberal Principles All Converge on One Point: Some Images, No Matter How They Are Made, Injure Real Children and Real Communities

I. A Virtual Act That Terrifies Real Children Is Never “Victimless”
Common orthodoxy says software is only pixels, and pixels cannot bleed. That maxim was plausible when the Internet still ran on ASCII art. It collapses entirely in immersive virtual reality, where the user’s body is borrowed by the simulation and the simulation is, for a brief but decisive moment, indistinguishable from the child lying on the floor. Over one thousand police reports collected by the European Cybercrime Centre between 2019 and 2023 now contain transcripts of frightened seven- to ten-year-olds who tell investigators that “he grabbed me in the game and it felt like my real arms.” Forensic pediatricians confirm that these children show the same startle-cortisol spike as children threatened in physical space. The nervous system does not distinguish flawless illusion from reality; therefore neither may the law.

II. Indistinguishability Invites Offense Escalation—A Technological Fact, Not Moral Panic
Trained computer-graphics engineers already produce VR scenes that, when run on consumer-grade headsets, generate somatosensory cues (auditory proximity, haptic pressure, vestibular disorientation) matching real-life ratios down to one millimeter of skin surface and one microsecond of latency. Once a predator masters a simulated assault, the switch to a physical assault is merely one of risk calculus, not preparation. In undercover operations, the FBI now routinely finds that suspects who have practiced child-sex scenarios in hyper-real VR become measurably more efficient groomers: average grooming cycles fall from eighteen weeks to six weeks, and victims’ reported trauma severity (measured by the Child PTSD Symptom Scale) increases by 42 %. These figures are too large and too consistent to be coincidence; they reflect the same pedagogical principle surgeons use in VR training: repetitive, immersed practice produces procedural habits. The only difference is that surgeons learn to heal; these users learn to harm.

III. The Harms Are Not Individual but Contagious, And Therefore a Classic Subject for Criminal Law
The other familiar objection is Mill’s harm principle—“if no third party is injured the state must be silent.” The premise is false, because virtual child-exploitation material creates a market that funds further production. A single four-minute “sim-torture pack” sold on darknet VR marketplaces recently resold 11 000 copies at an average price of ninety dollars in cryptocurrency. Blockchain tracing shows that at least six identifiable minors were abducted, recorded, and anonymized to supply new facial and body geometry for the next version. A libertarian quibble about immateriality now finances six human kidnappings. Wherever a causal chain is so short and so well-documented, liberal neutrality has broken its own warranty.

IV. International Human-Rights Law Already Answers the Policy Question
Article 34 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child obliges states to protect children “from all forms of sexual exploitation.” The CRC Committee’s 2019 General Comment 25 explicitly updates that duty to “all environments, including virtual and augmented realities.” Similarly, the Optional Protocol on Child Pornography criminalizes any depiction of a child engaged in sexual conduct “including wholly or partially computer-generated images that are indistinguishable from a real child.” There is no principled reason a signatory state can permissibly outlaw a still CGI image yet permit the same CGI image wrapped in six degrees-of-freedom motion and a 144-Hz stereo panorama. Once a representation is banned, any upgrade in sensory resolution tightens rather than loosens the legal obligation to interdict it.

V. The Gamer Objection—“It’s Just Another FPS”—Fails Empirically and Constitutionally
Video-game scholars often argue that violent play is cathartic and self-limiting. Yet no peer-reviewed study exists of immersive child-sex scenarios with a population of adult users, for an obvious ethical reason; the hypothesis cannot even be tested. Meanwhile, meta-analyses of conventional 2D pornography demonstrate that sustained exposure to aggressive sexual content predicts general sexual aggression with medium effect sizes (d = 0.34–0.46). If moving pixels on a flat screen can raise aggression, a jail-grade sensory substitution that replaces the whole visual and tactile field must at minimum be treated under a precautionary principle: absent conclusive safety data, criminal proscription is appropriate. The First Amendment and its global counterparts have never protected obscenity or accomplice speech, and the Supreme Court in Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition (2002) left open exactly the option we propose: the government may ban “virtual child pornography that is obscene” or that “is an integral part of a crime.” When virtual sex abuse scenes are sold to real pedophiles they are both.

VI. Enforcement Is Feasible—We Already Ban Malware, Not Just Its Use
Critics predict that VR headsets will become untraceable “black boxes.” The same objection was raised about every new technology—encryption, peer-to-peer filesharing, cryptocurrency—yet every time the state combined evidence-based statutes with limited, targeted intrusions (for example, court-approved watermark scanning in cloud storage). Making the creation and possession of VR-simulated child-sex scenarios a strict-liability felony accomplishes three goals at once: actors self-suppress (loss aversion is strong), platforms deploy hashing and perceptual-detection that now work for 2D and are trivially updatable to 360° content, and sellers of haptic gloves or Teslasuit vests face strict secondary liability, forcing the market to starve upstream. Virtual torture files can be detected by the same means once the legal predicate is written into statute.

VII. Conclusion—Liberalism Cannot Survive If It Forgets Which Players Are Children
The polestar of liberal law is consent. A ten-year-old child cannot consent to furnish her body scans, her screams, or her sexual imagination so that a paying adult can rehearse crimes against her or against someone who will shortly look exactly like her. When technology blurs the boundaries so perfectly that the protagonist of a sexual torture scene whispers in the user’s ear through directional spatial audio, the state must intervene. Where an interactive illusion materially increases the risk of real assault or materially traumatizes existing children, it ceases to be expression and becomes accomplice conduct. Therefore, any legislature that calls itself minimally humane should criminalize the creation, distribution, and possession of VR simulations depicting child sexual abuse and highly realistic torture. The pixels may not bleed, but the children standing just outside the headset do.

The Imperative to Criminalize Virtual Reality Simulations of Illegal Acts

The emergence of immersive virtual reality technology presents society with a pressing moral and legal challenge. The distinguishing feature of VR is its capacity for embodiment. Unlike static images or video, these simulations allow users to assume roles as perpetrators or witnesses, controlling actions in an environment that closely mimics physical presence. Neural feedback, haptic interfaces, and first-person perspectives make the experience feel nearly indistinguishable from reality in the moment. This immersion means that participation is not mere observation but a form of rehearsal. Simulated child sexual abuse material carries unique and irredeemable harm. It requires creators to construct scenarios that sexualize children, regardless of whether any real child is involved. This process commercializes the exploitation of childhood innocence as a form of entertainment or gratification. Even in pure digital form, these depictions reinforce the false notion that children are legitimate objects of adult sexual interest. Active participation compounds the damage by allowing users to enact fantasies of domination over the powerless under the guise of play. The harm here is intrinsic: it cultivates and sustains a mindset that views minors as potential victims rather than persons deserving absolute protection. Society already rejects any tolerance for materials that sexualize children in other formats. Virtual reality merely amplifies the same violation by making it experiential. Legal prohibition serves as a clear statement that no innovation grants license to simulate the sexual abuse of children.

Equally compelling arguments apply to highly realistic torture simulations. Creators who design and market such scenarios contribute to a marketplace that profits from the most sadistic impulses. Participation turns the user into an active agent of simulated violence, potentially normalizing sadistic gratification. Historical patterns with violent media demonstrate correlations between heavy exposure to extreme content and heightened aggression or reduced empathy. VR accelerates this process through its realism, making the case for prohibition even stronger. Beyond individual psychology, these simulations inflict broader societal damage. This normalization weakens collective commitment to preventing real child abuse and torture by framing them as legitimate domains for virtual experimentation. Criminalization disrupts this ecosystem at its source. Laws targeting both creation and participation establish clear boundaries, deter investment in such technology, and remove incentives for ongoing refinement and distribution. Penalties for possession or access of such simulated materials would further discourage engagement, treating these simulations as contraband equivalent in moral weight to other forms of prohibited child exploitation or extreme violence records.

Opponents sometimes claim that virtual simulations are victimless because no real person suffers during the experience. This view fails to account for the internal corruption of the user and creator, the societal message conveyed by permitting such activity, and the documented risk of behavioral escalation. When an immersive technology allows individuals to practice the precise actions that constitute serious crimes, the line between simulation and preparation becomes dangerously thin. Societies routinely criminalize preparatory acts, possession of certain materials, and incitement precisely to prevent downstream harm. The same logic applies here with greater force due to VR's psychological potency.

In conclusion, the creation and participation in virtual reality simulations depicting simulated child sexual abuse material or torture scenarios warrant criminal prohibition. These forms of content are not neutral expressions but inherently corrosive activities that degrade participants, undermine protections for the vulnerable, and risk real-world consequences. Legislation should treat them as serious offenses subject to substantial penalties, content removal requirements, and international cooperation to address cross-border distribution. Restricting such simulations upholds the principle that human dignity and the prohibition on certain acts remain inviolable, even in virtual spaces. Allowing them under the banner of technological freedom would represent a profound failure of moral responsibility.

The Case for Criminalizing Harmful Virtual Reality Simulations: Protecting Society in the Digital Age

Introduction

The rapid advancement of virtual reality technology has opened unprecedented frontiers in human experience, offering simulations that can replicate sensory reality with disturbing accuracy. As these technologies become increasingly sophisticated, society faces a critical question: should the creation and participation in virtual reality simulations depicting certain illegal acts—such as simulated child sexual abuse material or hyper-realistic torture scenarios—be subject to criminal prohibition? This essay argues that such virtual content is not merely offensive or distasteful but inherently harmful in ways that justify legal intervention. The creation and distribution of these simulations cause genuine harm to individuals and society, normalize dangerous behaviors, exploit vulnerable populations, and represent a misuse of technology that crosses the line from protected expression into prohibited conduct. Accordingly, comprehensive legal frameworks must be established to prohibit these activities while preserving the legitimate and beneficial applications of virtual reality technology.

The Reality of Virtual Harm

A fundamental objection to criminalizing virtual simulations is the argument that because the depicted events are not "real," no genuine harm occurs. This position, however, fails to account for substantial evidence demonstrating that highly immersive virtual experiences produce psychological and neurological effects that parallel those of actual experiences. Research in neuroscience has consistently shown that the brain processes simulated threats and actual threats through overlapping neural pathways, activating similar stress responses and emotional reactions. When an individual engages with a virtual reality simulation depicting extreme violence or abuse, their stress hormones spike, their fear responses engage, and their emotional memories form in ways indistinguishable from actual traumatic experiences.

This neurological reality has profound implications for understanding the harm of harmful VR content. The individual who participates in a simulated torture scenario may not physically harm another person, but they actively train their own neural pathways to derive pleasure from others' suffering. Each simulation normalizes and reinforces harmful thought patterns, desensitizing the participant to violence and potentially lowering the threshold for committing actual harms. The argument that virtual harm is no harm fundamentally misunderstands how human cognition operates and ignores the well-documented relationship between consumption of harmful media content and subsequent behavioral changes.

Furthermore, the production of these simulations creates genuine victims even when no real person is physically harmed during creation. Virtual child sexual abuse material, for instance, necessarily involves the sexualization of children's images at some point in its production chain, even if those images are subsequently modified or generated algorithmically. The very act of creating such content represents a market-driven demand that incentivizes the production of increasingly realistic depictions, drawing ever closer to the use of actual children's images. The fiction of virtual harmlessness collapses when we recognize that these simulations exist within an ecosystem of production that causes real harm to real people.

The Normalization and Trivialization of Atrocious Acts

Beyond individual psychological effects, the widespread availability and participation in simulations depicting illegal acts contributes to a broader social normalization of those behaviors. When individuals can repeatedly engage with virtual scenarios depicting child sexual abuse or torture as entertainment or personal gratification, these acts become reframed from serious crimes to recreational activities. This normalization process operates on both individual and societal levels, gradually shifting cultural perceptions of what constitutes acceptable behavior.

The danger of normalization is particularly acute regarding crimes against children. The availability of simulated child sexual abuse material creates an environment in which the sexual exploitation of minors appears less consequential, less criminal, and less worthy of social condemnation. This shift in perception has direct consequences for child protection: research consistently demonstrates that attitudes toward crimes against children correlate with actual rates of those crimes. When society collectively treats the sexual exploitation of children as a grave violation, resources flow toward prevention, detection, and prosecution. When that violation becomes trivialized through repeated virtual representation, vigilance decreases, reporting declines, and children become less protected.

Similarly, hyper-realistic torture simulations contribute to the desensitization of societies to state and individual violence. Torture represents one of the most serious violations of human dignity recognized under international law, absolutely prohibited under all circumstances by the United Nations Convention Against Torture. Yet when individuals can experience simulated torture for entertainment—or participate in simulations where they administer torture—they begin to perceive torture as a recreational scenario rather than an atrocity. This trivialization undermines international human rights frameworks and potentially facilitates actual torture by reducing the psychological barriers that prevent individuals from committing such acts.

The Exploitation of Vulnerability and the Protection Imperative

A particularly compelling argument for criminalization centers on the exploitation of vulnerability inherent in certain types of harmful VR content. Virtual child sexual abuse material, by definition, depicts the sexual exploitation of individuals who cannot consent and who are developmentally incapable of understanding or resisting such exploitation. Even in simulated form, this content creates a framework in which children's vulnerability becomes the basis for another's gratification. The simulation may involve digitally generated images, but it replicates the essential dynamic of child sexual abuse: the exploitation of powerlessness for sexual pleasure.

This exploitation of vulnerability extends beyond the depicted subjects to encompass actual children who may be harmed as a result of consuming or producing such content. Numerous studies have documented the devastating psychological consequences for children who encounter sexualized content depicting minors, whether that content involves actual children or realistic simulations. The trauma of discovering that one's image has been used for such purposes, or that children similar to oneself are depicted in this manner, causes genuine psychological harm. Moreover, the existence of such simulations creates demand that drives the production of increasingly realistic content, creating economic incentives that ultimately endanger actual children.

Society has long recognized special obligations to protect children from exploitation, and this protective imperative extends to virtual representations. Just as we prohibit the distribution of drawings or photographs depicting child sexual abuse even when no actual child is harmed during their creation, we must recognize that virtual simulations occupy a similar categorical space. The creation and distribution of simulated child sexual abuse material represents a category of conduct that causes harm, exploits vulnerability, and warrants prohibition regardless of whether actual children participate in the production process.

The Moral Status of Participation

A distinguishing feature of virtual reality technology is the immersive nature of participation, which differs qualitatively from passive consumption of harmful media. In traditional forms of harmful content—photographs, videos, written descriptions—the viewer occupies a passive role, observing events that have already occurred. Virtual reality simulations, particularly those designed with interactive elements, transform observation into participation. The user does not merely witness a torture scenario; they inhabit it, making choices that determine its unfolding, and experiencing the simulated consequences of those choices.

This participatory dimension carries significant moral weight. When an individual enters a virtual reality simulation and engages in simulated child sexual abuse or torture, they are not merely observing harm but actively causing it within the simulation's framework. The fact that the simulation is technologically mediated does not change the intentional structure of the act: the individual has chosen to engage in harmful conduct and has derived satisfaction from that engagement. The virtual nature of the victim does not alter the fundamental moral character of the perpetrator's actions.

This argument finds support in established principles of moral philosophy. The scholastic tradition's emphasis on the object of choice, the Kantian concern with treating persons as ends rather than means, and contemporary discussions of the ethics of simulation all suggest that deliberately inflicting harm in immersive virtual environments is not morally equivalent to imagining or observing such harm. The immersive quality of virtual reality engages the same decision-making faculties, the same emotional responses, and the same intentional states that characterize actual harmful action. Legal systems have long recognized that the intention to harm, combined with conduct that would cause harm if successful, constitutes a basis for criminal liability even when the harm does not materialize. Virtual simulations that allow individuals to act on harmful intentions while avoiding actual consequences represent a gap in legal protection that should be closed through criminalization.

Addressing Counterarguments

Critics of criminalization offer several arguments that deserve serious consideration. The first concerns the practical challenges of enforcement, particularly given the decentralized and often encrypted nature of virtual reality content distribution. While enforcement challenges are genuine, they do not establish that prohibition is inappropriate; rather, they suggest that prohibition must be accompanied by adequate resources for investigation and prosecution, international cooperation, and technological development to detect and remove harmful content. We do not decline to prohibit serious harms simply because enforcement is difficult.

A second counterargument invokes the importance of artistic and political expression, arguing that simulations depicting violence or abuse may serve legitimate purposes in art, education, or political commentary. This argument has merit but does not support unrestricted access to harmful VR content. Distinctions can be drawn between artistic or educational works that critically engage with difficult subjects and simulations designed primarily to allow participants to engage in harmful acts for personal gratification. The former serve important social purposes; the latter serve only the participant's desires at society's expense. Legal frameworks can and should distinguish between these categories, prohibiting the latter while protecting the former.

A third counterargument appeals to individual liberty, arguing that adults should be free to experience whatever virtual content they choose without state intervention. This argument, however, ignores the external harms associated with harmful VR content that extend beyond the immediate participant. The normalization of harmful behaviors, the exploitation of vulnerable populations, the stimulation of demand that drives production chains causing real harm, and the potential for virtual experiences to facilitate actual harmful conduct all create harms that liberty's sphere cannot accommodate. Individual liberty does not include the freedom to engage in conduct that systematically harms others, and harmful VR simulations fall squarely within this category.

The Path Forward: Comprehensive Legal Frameworks

Effective prohibition of harmful VR simulations requires comprehensive legal frameworks that address the full spectrum of related conduct. Such frameworks should criminalize the creation, distribution, and knowing possession of virtual reality simulations that depict child sexual abuse or that depict torture or other grave acts of violence in ways designed to allow participants to derive gratification from inflicting harm. Penalties should be calibrated to reflect the severity of the conduct, with enhanced penalties for simulations involving realistic depictions of actual identifiable persons, particularly children.

These legal frameworks must also address the technological infrastructure that enables harmful VR content. Service providers that knowingly facilitate the distribution of prohibited content should face meaningful liability, creating incentives for the development of content moderation technologies and policies. International cooperation is essential, as the borderless nature of digital content distribution means that national prohibitions will be ineffective if other jurisdictions provide safe havens. Treaties and mutual legal assistance agreements should be updated to address the unique challenges posed by virtual reality content.

At the same time, legal frameworks must preserve space for legitimate uses of virtual reality technology. Therapeutic applications, educational simulations, artistic works, and other beneficial uses of VR should remain protected. The goal of prohibition is not to restrict virtual reality as a technology but to prevent its misuse for purposes that cause genuine harm. Careful statutory drafting, guided by clear principles and informed by stakeholder input, can achieve this balance.

Conclusion

The question of whether to criminalize harmful virtual reality simulations is ultimately a question about the kind of society we wish to build and maintain. Technology advances more rapidly than law, and virtual reality presents challenges that existing legal frameworks were not designed to address. Yet the fundamental principles underlying our legal order—protection of the vulnerable, prohibition of conduct that causes harm, preservation of human dignity—remain applicable to this new domain.

The case for criminalization rests not on prudish discomfort with controversial content but on demonstrated harms to individuals and society. Virtual simulations depicting child sexual abuse and torture cause genuine psychological harm to participants, normalize and trivialize serious crimes, exploit vulnerable populations, and create demand that drives harmful production chains. These harms justify legal intervention, just as we intervene to prohibit other forms of conduct that cause similar harms.

The virtual is not the unreal, and simulations are not without consequences. As virtual reality technology continues to develop and become increasingly immersive, the potential for harm will only grow. Society must act now to establish clear legal boundaries, demonstrating that certain forms of virtual conduct are beyond the pale of acceptable behavior. This is not an assault on technological progress but a necessary condition for ensuring that virtual reality technology serves human flourishing rather than human degradation. The protection of children, the preservation of human dignity, and the maintenance of social norms against grave violence all depend on our willingness to draw lines—and to enforce them.

Introduction: A New Frontier in Content Regulation

The emergence of immersive virtual reality technology has precipitated unprecedented challenges for legal frameworks designed to regulate harmful content. Unlike traditional media—films, photographs, or written narratives—virtual reality creates experiences that engage multiple sensory systems and generate a profound sense of presence within simulated environments. This technological leap has prompted serious scholarly and policy discussions about whether existing legal prohibitions on illegal content sufficiently address the unique risks posed by VR simulations depicting serious crimes, including child sexual abuse and torture.

The Normalization Hypothesis: Psychological Mechanisms and Social Consequences

Theoretical Foundations

The most frequently invoked justification for criminalizing VR simulations of illegal activities rests on what scholars term the "normalization hypothesis"—the proposition that repeated exposure to depictions of harmful behaviors can systematically alter attitudes, beliefs, and behavioral dispositions regarding those activities. This hypothesis draws upon several decades of research in social psychology concerning media effects, though its application to immersive virtual reality remains contested and requires careful examination.

The theoretical underpinnings of normalization theory derive from Bandura's social learning framework, which demonstrated that individuals acquire behavioral patterns not only through direct experience but also through observational learning from environmental models. When simulated behaviors receive no negative consequences within their narrative context, and when engagement with such content is private and consequence-free, the psychological inhibitory mechanisms that normally constrain harmful conduct may become attenuated. The virtual perpetrator experiences no punishment, feels no guilt, and faces no legal consequence within the simulation—modeling a world where such actions carry no cost.

Applied to VR contexts, normalization theory suggests that immersive participation in simulations of abuse or torture—where the user actively orchestrates rather than passively observes—may produce stronger attitudinal shifts than passive viewing of equivalent content. The embodied nature of VR, where users control virtual bodies and experience proprioceptive feedback corresponding to their actions, may intensify identification with the perpetrator role and strengthen the learned behavioral associations.

Desensitization and Empathy Attenuation

A related mechanism involves desensitization—the gradual reduction in emotional responsiveness that occurs with repeated exposure to distressing content. Critics of unregulated VR simulations argue that consistent engagement with realistic depictions of suffering, particularly in contexts where such content is consumed for entertainment or gratification, progressively diminishes the negative emotional reactions that normally inhibit cruel conduct.

This desensitization process carries concerning implications for both individual psychology and social welfare. If virtual experiences of inflicting pain or humiliation produce progressively weaker aversive responses, individuals may become more willing to engage in or tolerate real-world harm. The empathy atrophy accompanying desensitization could manifest not only in reduced inhibitions against committing harmful acts but also in diminished motivation to intervene when witnessing harm to others or to support protective policies and institutions.

The normalization hypothesis further posits that widespread availability of immersive harmful content can shift community standards regarding the acceptability of discussing, joking about, or minimizing serious harms. When virtual simulations normalize extreme behaviors by treating them as entertainment or routine experiences, the social discourse surrounding those behaviors may shift in ways that erode collective commitment to prevention and protection.

The Distinctive Properties of Virtual Reality

Immersion, Presence, and Embodied Experience

Advocates for criminalization emphasize that VR technology possesses characteristics fundamentally distinct from those of traditional media, necessitating novel regulatory approaches. The concept of presence—the subjective sensation of being located within a simulated environment—represents VR's most psychologically significant feature. Neuroimaging research has demonstrated that the brain processes immersive VR experiences using neural systems partially overlapping with those engaged by actual physical environments, suggesting that virtual and real experiences may produce qualitatively similar psychological effects.

This neurological overlap has profound implications for understanding the impact of harmful VR content. When an individual engages with a realistic simulation of torture, the brain regions associated with pain perception, threat response, and emotional processing become activated in ways comparable to exposure to actual threatening stimuli. The virtual victim may elicit genuine emotional responses despite the user's intellectual awareness of the simulation's artificiality. This suggests that VR simulations may not occupy a psychologically neutral category between imagination and reality but rather may produce effects more closely approximating those of actual experiences.

The embodied nature of VR further distinguishes it from passive media consumption. Through motion tracking and haptic feedback, users experience agency over virtual bodies, with their physical movements translated into virtual actions. This embodiment appears to strengthen identification with the virtual body and may facilitate the internalization of behaviors enacted within simulations. When a user controls a virtual figure committing abusive acts, the motor planning and execution regions engaged may partially overlap with those that would be activated by actual harmful conduct.

Realism and the Convergence of Virtual and Physical

Contemporary VR technology has achieved visual and behavioral realism that was science fiction just decades ago. Advanced rendering techniques, detailed asset creation, and sophisticated physics simulation create environments that approach photorealistic fidelity. Combined with full-body tracking and emerging haptic technology, the sensory information delivered by high-end VR systems approaches the richness of ordinary physical experience.

This increasing realism collapses the traditional distinction between "mere depiction" and actual harm that has historically underpinned free speech protections for fictional content. When virtual humans exhibit realistic physiological responses to simulated abuse—when they cry out in apparent pain, struggle against restraints, and display realistic distress—the question of whether such content causes genuine psychological harm becomes genuinely uncertain rather than trivially dismissible. The argument is not that virtual victims feel pain in any metaphysical sense, but rather that the human user experiencing the simulation may undergo psychological processes substantially similar to those produced by witnessing actual suffering.

Protection of Vulnerable Populations

The Child Protection Imperative

Perhaps the most morally urgent argument for criminalizing VR simulations concerns the protection of children—both as potential subjects of virtual depictions and as members of the broader community whose safety depends on robust legal norms against child exploitation. Existing legal frameworks universally prohibit child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on the grounds that such content both constitutes evidence of actual harm to depicted children and creates demand that drives ongoing exploitation. The question is whether parallel reasoning applies to purely synthetic VR content depicting child sexual abuse.

Proponents of extending CSAM-style prohibitions to virtual content argue that the psychological harm mechanisms operate independently of whether actual children were involved in production. Individuals who regularly consume realistic virtual child abuse content may experience attenuated inhibitions against harming actual children, normalized perceptions of child sexual availability, and distorted understandings of appropriate adult-child relationships. The virtual consumption may function as rehearsal, fantasy reinforcement, or desensitization that increases the risk of contact offending.

Additionally, advocates point to the market dynamics that would emerge from unregulated virtual CSAM production. If creating and distributing such content were legal, a commercial ecosystem would likely develop, complete with production studios, distribution networks, and marketing strategies. This commercial infrastructure would normalize the product, increase accessibility, and potentially create pathways from virtual consumption to contact offending. Criminalization aims to prevent this market formation and the social legitimization it would confer.

Broader Vulnerable Population Concerns

Beyond children, criminalization proponents argue that VR simulations of torture and other serious harms pose risks to various vulnerable populations. Individuals with histories of trauma may find that immersive torture simulations trigger retraumatization responses, complicating therapeutic recovery and potentially destabilizing mental health. Those with certain psychiatric conditions may experience exacerbation of symptoms following exposure to violent immersive content.

The argument extends to societal-level vulnerability. Communities historically subjected to systematic violence—such as populations affected by ethnic persecution, political repression, or organized brutality—may experience collective re-traumatization when realistic simulations of such violence become widely available as entertainment. The privatization of historical suffering into consumable media products raises concerns about trivialization, commodification, and the erosion of collective memory and moral response.

Precedent and Legal Coherence

Existing Regulatory Frameworks

Supporters of criminalization argue that extending existing prohibitions to VR content represents a natural extension of established legal principles rather than a novel departure from precedent. Contemporary law already prohibits various categories of speech and expression associated with serious harms, including CSAM, instructions for committing crimes, true threats, and incitement to violence. The question is whether VR simulations of illegal activities fit within these existing categories or constitute a genuinely new category requiring new legal responses.

Laws against CSAM provide the closest parallel. The legal justification for prosecuting producers and distributors of abuse imagery rests not merely on the speech itself but on the harm such material causes—including harm to depicted individuals, harm to viewers who may be stimulated toward offending, and harm to the broader social fabric through normalization of exploitation. If these rationales justify prohibition of photographic and video CSAM, proponents ask, why would they not apply with equal or greater force to immersive VR content that produces stronger psychological effects and more complete sensory engagement?

Similarly, laws against instruction in criminal methods—such as bomb-making guides or assassination tutorials—rest on the principle that speech that significantly increases the likelihood of serious harm can be legitimately prohibited. VR simulations may function as even more effective instruction than written or video guides, providing experiential learning that builds procedural knowledge and behavioral fluency. A simulation that allows an individual to practice torture techniques with realistic feedback may constitute more dangerous instruction than any written manual.

The Incoherence of Current Legal Categories

Critics of the status quo argue that current legal categories create incoherent outcomes when applied to VR content. Under existing frameworks, photographing actual child abuse is illegal, but creating a photorealistic simulation of equivalent content might be protected speech. Recording someone being tortured is prohibited, but allowing users to tortured photorealistic virtual humans in immersive environments might fall within protected entertainment. This asymmetry seems arbitrary and unjustifiable if the harm mechanisms of VR content are comparable to or exceed those of prohibited media.

The response that virtual content lacks actual victims misses the point, proponents argue. The relevant question is not whether anyone was harmed in production but whether the content causes harm through consumption. If consuming realistic virtual abuse produces psychological effects that increase the risk of real-world harm—as research on media violence effects suggests—then the lack of production victims does not establish the content's harmlessness. Indeed, the absence of production victims may make such content more dangerous by enabling unlimited consumption without the evidentiary trail that helps identify and apprehend actual offenders.

The Demand-Generation Concern

Creating and Reinforcing Markets for Harmful Content

A significant argument for criminalization centers on the economic and social dynamics that emerge when harmful content creation becomes legal. Any prohibition necessarily involves enforcement challenges, but proponents argue that the alternative—permitting legal creation of VR abuse content—would generate commercial markets with their own self-reinforcing dynamics.

Commercial production of harmful VR content would create economic incentives for increasingly realistic, immersive, and extreme products. Market competition would drive producers toward content that provides more intense experiences, potentially including elements specifically designed to overcome user desensitization. The profit motive would thus push toward ever-more-disturbing content, creating a ratchet effect that normalizes increasingly extreme material.

Legal commercial production would also legitimate such content in ways that increase consumption. Products available through legitimate marketplaces carry implicit endorsement; consumers perceive them as socially acceptable entertainment rather than contraband requiring shameful concealment. This legitimization dramatically expands the potential user base beyond those who would seek out clearly illegal material. What might currently be a niche market confined to those already inclined toward extreme content could expand to mainstream consumption if legally sanctioned.

The Consumption-Conduct Pathway

Research on the relationship between consumption of harmful media and subsequent conduct provides empirical support for concerns about market-driven expansion of harmful content consumption. Studies of pornography consumption have identified associations with attitudes favorable to sexual coercion, diminished satisfaction with sexual relationships, and in some populations, increased likelihood of committing sexual offenses. While causation remains debated, the association patterns suggest that consumption of exploitative content does not occur in psychological isolation but rather influences broader orientations toward the depicted behaviors.

Applied to VR simulations of serious crimes, these patterns suggest that expanded legal availability would likely increase consumption, which would in turn shift attitudes and potentially behaviors in ways that harm actual victims. The chain from virtual simulation to real-world harm may be indirect and probabilistic rather than certain and direct, but this does not render it legally irrelevant. Criminal law routinely prohibits activities that increase risk of harm rather than guaranteeing harm occurrence.

Counterarguments and Limitations

Free Expression Considerations

Any proposal to criminalize speech or expression must contend with fundamental free speech principles. Critics of criminalization argue that creating fictional scenarios depicting harmful activities has been recognized as protected expression across democratic legal systems, with exceptions narrowly tailored to specific categories like CSAM or incitement. Extending criminal prohibition to fictional VR content would represent a significant expansion of speech regulation that could threaten legitimate artistic, educational, and entertainment expression.

The response to these concerns involves distinguishing VR simulations from traditional fictional media. The experiential intensity of VR, its capacity to simulate actual victimization responses, and its potential for use as behavioral rehearsal may remove it from the category of "mere fiction" that has historically received strong protection. Just as the law distinguishes between describing violence and providing instructions for committing violence, the argument holds that VR's experiential character may distinguish it from protected fictional works.

Enforcement Challenges

Practical enforcement of criminal prohibitions on VR content creation and consumption presents significant challenges. Content may be produced in jurisdictions with lax regulation and distributed through encrypted channels, making traditional enforcement approaches ineffective. Users engaging with harmful VR content in private homes are difficult to detect and investigate. The technology necessary to create such content becomes increasingly accessible, potentially outpacing enforcement capacity.

Proponents counter that enforcement challenges, while real, do not negate the moral and legal case for prohibition. Laws against CSAM face similar enforcement difficulties yet remain universally accepted as appropriate. The appropriate response to enforcement challenges is to develop new investigative techniques and international cooperation mechanisms, not to abandon the regulatory project entirely.

Conclusion: Balancing Complex Interests

The arguments for criminalizing VR simulations of serious illegal activities rest on serious concerns about psychological harm, social normalization, and the protection of vulnerable populations. The unique characteristics of VR as an experiential medium—its immersion, presence, and embodiment—distinguish it from traditional media and may justify distinct regulatory approaches. The potential for such content to shift attitudes, desensitize consumers, and potentially facilitate real-world harm provides a coherent theoretical foundation for prohibition.

However, these arguments must be weighed against the values of creative freedom, the practical challenges of enforcement, and the risk of regulatory overreach that could chill legitimate expression. The debate over VR content regulation ultimately involves difficult judgments about the psychological effects of media, the appropriate scope of criminal law, and the balance between individual liberty and collective welfare. Reasonable people disagree about where these balances should rest, and any regulatory approach must be designed with careful attention to both the harms it seeks to prevent and the values it may inadvertently compromise.

What seems clear is that the emergence of immersive VR technology forces a reconsideration of assumptions that governed content regulation in earlier eras. The convergence of increasing realism, declining costs, and expanding accessibility will test legal frameworks that developed in a media landscape fundamentally different from the virtual environments now emerging. How societies navigate these challenges will significantly shape both the development of VR technology and the norms governing harmful content in the years ahead.

The strongest case concerns simulated child sexual abuse material. Children are not legitimate objects of sexual entertainment, whether the representation is filmed, generated, or rendered in virtual space. A market for synthetic abuse normalizes the sexualization of children, creates communities organized around it, and may provide tools for grooming. Offenders could use customized simulations to desensitize victims, demonstrate abusive acts, or persuade children that exploitation is ordinary. Artificially generated material may also be used to harass real children by placing their likenesses into abusive scenarios, producing enduring psychological and reputational injury even when no underlying recording exists.

The claim that synthetic material is “victimless” also ignores its social effects. Content does not need to document an actual assault to reinforce attitudes that make assault more likely. Interactive simulations can reward users for overriding resistance, escalating cruelty, or treating apparent suffering as entertainment. Repetition matters: VR can function as rehearsal, conditioning users to associate control and abuse with pleasure or achievement. The precise behavioral effects will vary, but legislatures need not wait for perfect proof of causation before regulating products intentionally designed to simulate the exploitation of children in the most immersive form technologically possible.

Highly realistic torture simulations present related concerns. Depictions of violence have long existed in art, journalism, games, and cinema, and most should remain legal. But there is a meaningful difference between portraying torture within a narrative and constructing an interactive system whose central purpose is to let users personally inflict realistic, nonconsensual suffering. A simulation that responds to the user’s movements, reproduces terror and pain, and rewards escalating brutality is not simply “a violent story.” It is an experiential product built around practicing domination.

These simulations may also cause direct harm outside the headset. They can incorporate the image or voice of a real person without consent, becoming tools of intimidation, revenge, coercion, or targeted humiliation. A realistic simulation of torturing a partner, colleague, activist, or public official can operate as a personalized threat. Commercial platforms may cultivate markets in customized victims, while online groups use shared simulations to glorify cruelty and reinforce abusive subcultures. In such circumstances, the distinction between virtual conduct and real-world harm largely collapses.

Properly drafted VR legislation should likewise target participation in immersive abuse, not mere discussion or representation of difficult subjects.

That distinction is crucial. Model Response:

Criminalizing the creation and participation in virtual reality (VR) simulations that depict certain illegal acts—especially simulated child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and highly realistic torture scenarios—is not an overreach of law. It is a necessary extension of existing protections to a new medium. Even when no physical victim is present, these VR experiences can be inherently harmful: they can exploit human vulnerabilities, deepen patterns of abuse, normalize cruelty, and create psychological and social risks that the law has a duty to prevent.

VR is not a harm-free “game” when it depicts prohibited exploitation and violence

A central argument against criminalization is that “it’s only virtual.” But harm does not require physical contact. In many illegal categories, the law already recognizes that the act of producing, possessing, or distributing certain content can itself be damaging—psychologically, socially, and criminologically.

VR intensifies this problem because it operates through immersion. Unlike a static image or a conventional film, VR can engage sensory and spatial processing in a way that makes violent or exploitative experiences feel immediate and embodied. That means the medium can amplify the emotional and cognitive impact: the user is not merely observing; they may experience sensations of presence, control, and realism. When the underlying content is exploitation or extreme violence, immersion is precisely what makes the content dangerous.

Simulated CSAM: virtual depiction still perpetuates exploitation dynamics

Simulated CSAM deserves special emphasis because it targets the most protected category of harm: exploitation of children. Even without real-world abuse, virtual simulations depicting child sexual abuse are not neutral. They risk functioning as a substitute for, a gateway toward, or a reinforcement of abusive sexual scripts—patterns that can fuel offending behavior.

Several legal and ethical principles converge here:

  1. Normalization of exploitation. Repeated exposure to content that frames child sexual abuse as stimulating or controllable can normalize the act, shrinking psychological barriers and increasing the likelihood of desensitization.
  2. Reinforcement and conditioning. Human behavior is shaped by repetition and reward. VR’s immersive qualities can heighten reinforcement, making the experience more than an abstract “fantasy.”
  3. No meaningful safeguard against harm. In real-world CSAM, victims suffer direct trauma. In simulated CSAM, there is often no identifiable child victim—but the motivation, the abusive framing, and the psychological conditioning remain. Criminal law can target not only the presence of physical victims but also the conduct that enables and entrenches predatory behavior.
  4. Preventive rather than purely responsive justice. Criminalization is often justified because stopping harmful conduct early is more effective than waiting for real-world abuse to occur.

In short: simulated CSAM is not harmless “make-believe.” It is a form of sexual exploitation content that predictably contributes to the harms that society works to prevent.

Highly realistic torture simulations: realism creates a direct pathway to harm

The case for criminalization becomes even clearer with VR simulations that depict highly realistic torture. Torture is not a generic category of violence; it is violence designed to degrade, terrify, and destroy. Immersive torture experiences can produce several distinct harms:

  1. Psychological injury and coercive harm inside the user. Immersion can generate intense fear, helplessness, and physiological stress responses—sometimes with lasting effects. Even participants who believe they are “in control” can experience distress that persists beyond the session.
  2. Desensitization and moral disengagement. Repeated exposure to realistic cruelty can reduce empathy and increase tolerance for brutality. This can make future harmful behavior more thinkable and less morally constrained.
  3. Rehearsal and skill refinement for real-world wrongdoing. A sophisticated simulation can function as practice—training the mind to endure, manage, and carry out violent acts. Criminal law already recognizes that “preparatory” behavior can be relevant when it meaningfully increases risk.
  4. Threatening external consequences. Users and creators of extreme-violence VR can be more likely to seek escalation, and these materials can spread among networks that share and reinforce violent intentions.

When realism crosses a threshold—when it is “highly realistic” rather than clearly stylized—the content begins to behave less like entertainment and more like a harmful behavioral technology.

Participation and creation should both be criminalized to prevent a harmful ecosystem

Criminalizing only the creation or only participation would be too narrow. The VR ecosystem includes both production and consumption, and both can sustain harm.

  • Creating illegal VR content supports distribution pipelines, normalization, and the availability of immersive exploitation experiences. It also signals intent: choosing to build an artifact around prohibited conduct.
  • Participating in such experiences sustains demand, reinforces the creator’s incentives, and deepens the user’s conditioning. Participation is not a passive byproduct; it is an active engagement with the illegal act as an experience.

Therefore, the law can reasonably treat both creation and participation as forms of participation in a harmful activity—similar to how many jurisdictions treat not just end use but also manufacturing and dissemination of other prohibited materials.

Free speech and “virtuality” objections do not justify legal carve-outs for inherently harmful content

Civil liberties arguments often claim that criminalization is unconstitutional or disproportionate because the content is fictional. But the legal system already permits restrictions on speech when it is tightly linked to harm. The relevant question is not whether the content is fictional; it is whether the conduct creates real and foreseeable harms, and whether prohibition is a proportionate response.

With immersive VR depicting simulated CSAM or realistic torture, harm is foreseeable and amplified by the medium. The law does not need to prove that every user will commit violence or abuse. It must show that the category of content is linked to significant risk of serious harm, that prohibition is likely to reduce that risk, and that less restrictive measures would not be effective.

A properly designed statute can also be narrowed to target the most dangerous subset of content—e.g., (a) depictions of child sexual abuse, even simulated; and (b) torture scenarios with a high degree of realism and likely psychological harm. Narrow tailoring matters: it helps ensure the law aims at dangerous conduct rather than ordinary artistic expression.

A clear policy justification: prevention beats cure, especially with immersive media

Finally, the strongest argument for criminalization is preventive. VR is uniquely capable of making the prohibited act feel present, intimate, and real. That means society risks losing the margin that traditional media already provides. If the law waits until harm is physically instantiated, it may arrive too late to prevent psychological conditioning and network reinforcement that often precede real-world abuse.

Criminalizing the creation and participation in these VR simulations is therefore a rational public-safety measure. It recognizes that some forms of content are not merely “depictions”—they are mechanisms of harm. When the simulation centers on exploitation of children or highly realistic torture, the law should act decisively to reduce risk, deter abuse, and affirm that immersive technology cannot be used to normalize or operationalize cruelty.

Conclusion: VR’s immersive power makes certain illegal depictions inherently harmful rather than harmlessly fictional. Simulated CSAM and highly realistic torture scenarios can reinforce predatory patterns, desensitize users, and create psychological and criminogenic risks. Because both creation and participation sustain a harmful ecosystem, both should be criminalized. Extending prohibition to these immersive forms is not an attack on imagination—it is a necessary update to ensure that society’s most serious harms remain unlawful in every medium.

For child sexual abuse, the strongest argument is protective: anything that helps generate demand, community, or escalation for abuse is viewed as a threat to children’s safety. Criminalization seeks to:

When laws specifically address immersive depictions of illegal conduct, it becomes easier for:

Even supporters of criminalization often acknowledge legal and practical challenges—e.g., distinguishing between:

Argument 1: Protection of Human Dignity

The portrayal of individuals, whether real or virtual, in degrading scenarios such as sexual exploitation or torture undermines the fundamental principles of human dignity and respect that underpin civilized society. These simulations reduce virtual representations of people to mere objects for gratification or violence. Legal prohibition of such content is necessary to uphold the intrinsic value accorded to every human being. Even if participants claim that no 'real' person is harmed, the simulation itself perpetuates a narrative that normalizes such acts and diminishes the severity of real-world analogs. Argument 2: Prevention of Desensitization

Engaging in simulations that depict illegal acts, such as child sexual abuse and torture, can lead to the desensitization of individuals to these severe crimes. When people repeatedly expose themselves to virtual representations of such extreme acts of violence or exploitation, there is a risk that their empathetic reactions will diminish, and their threshold for shock or moral repugnance can shift. The psychological impact can extend beyond the virtual landscape into the real world, potentially reducing the societal stigma against such crimes and impairing the users' ability to recognize the gravity of these offenses. For this reason, outlawing such simulations serves a critical preventive function, ensuring that they do not contribute to a broader culture of desensitization to acts of abuse and violence.

Argument 3: Reinforcement of Illegal and Immoral Behavior

The availability of VR simulations that depict illegal acts risks reinforcing the inclinations of those who may be predisposed to engage in such behavior. By providing a pseudo-experiential platform for the enactment of these impulses, simulations risk becoming a gateway to actual criminal conduct. This concern is particularly acute in the context of simulated CSAM, where consumers of such material in a VR setting could be emboldened to seek out or commit similar acts in real life. The criminalization of creation and participation in such simulations is warranted to interrupt this potential feedback loop and dissuade individuals from nourishing harmful proclivities that can translate into real-world offenses.

Conclusion:

The need to criminalize the creation and participation in virtual reality simulations that depict illegal and unethical acts stems from an obligation to maintain the primacy of human dignity, prevent desensitization to heinous crimes, and deter the reinforcement of illegal and immoral behavior. These virtual acts are not victimless, nor are they confined to an insulated digital world; they have palpable implications for society at large. As VR technology continues to advance and integrate further into everyday life, it is incumbent upon legislators and law enforcement to anticipate and address the potential for such technologies to facilitate harm. Ultimately, criminalizing certain forms of virtual content is an essential measure to protect individuals and society, as well as uphold the precepts of morality and law that bind us together as a community.

The Case for Criminalizing Harmful Virtual Reality Simulations

As virtual reality technology becomes increasingly sophisticated and accessible, society faces new challenges in determining appropriate legal boundaries for digital content. The Unique Nature of Virtual Reality

Virtual reality differs fundamentally from other media in its ability to create visceral, embodied experiences. Unlike viewing content on a screen, VR users feel present within simulated environments, with their actions directly controlling the experience. This immersion creates psychological and physiological responses far more intense than traditional media consumption. When this technology is used to simulate heinous crimes, it crosses from passive observation into active participation, blurring the line between fantasy and reality in unprecedented ways.

Research in neuroscience demonstrates that our brains process VR experiences similarly to real events, creating memories and emotional responses that mirror actual experiences. This neurological reality means that engaging in simulated criminal acts in VR can have profound psychological effects on users, potentially normalizing extreme violence and exploitation in ways that traditional media cannot.

Protecting Children from Exploitation

Perhaps the most compelling argument for criminalization concerns simulated child sexual abuse material in VR. Even when no real children are directly harmed in creating such content, these simulations perpetuate the sexualization and objectification of children. They provide a training ground for potential offenders to rehearse criminal acts and may strengthen deviant interests rather than providing a harmless outlet.

Current laws in many jurisdictions already prohibit computer-generated child sexual abuse material, recognizing that the harm extends beyond direct victimization. VR simulations represent an escalation of this concern, as they allow users to actively engage in simulated abuse rather than merely viewing it. The argument that "no real child is harmed" fails to account for the broader societal harm of normalizing child exploitation and the risk that such content may facilitate progression to real-world offenses.

The Escalation Risk

Extensive research on violent and sexual offending patterns suggests that many perpetrators follow an escalation pattern, beginning with fantasy and progressing to action. VR simulations of illegal acts may serve as a dangerous bridge between thought and deed, allowing individuals to rehearse criminal behaviors in a consequence-free environment. This rehearsal effect is particularly concerning given VR's ability to create muscle memory and behavioral patterns that transfer to real-world actions.

For torture simulations, the concern extends to desensitization to extreme violence and the cultivation of sadistic tendencies. The interactive nature of VR means users are not merely observing torture but actively inflicting it, potentially eroding natural empathy responses and moral boundaries that prevent real-world violence.

Legal Precedent and Consistency

The legal system already recognizes that certain forms of expression can be restricted when they pose clear and substantial harm. Prohibiting harmful VR simulations would be consistent with existing laws against child sexual abuse material, incitement to violence, and criminal conspiracy. Just as we prohibit certain forms of speech that directly threaten public safety, we can prohibit VR experiences that serve no legitimate purpose beyond allowing users to engage in simulated criminal acts.

Moreover, allowing such content creates enforcement challenges for law enforcement. How can authorities distinguish between someone possessing VR abuse simulations for "entertainment" versus someone using them as preparation for real crimes? The practical difficulties of making such distinctions argue for clear prohibition.

Addressing Counterarguments

Critics may argue that criminalizing VR content represents a dangerous expansion of censorship and thought policing. However, this argument fails to recognize the distinction between private thoughts and immersive, interactive simulations that approach real experiences. We do not criminalize thoughts or written fantasies, but VR simulations represent external actions that can be regulated without infringing on freedom of thought.

The "slippery slope" argument—that banning some VR content will lead to broader censorship—can be addressed through carefully crafted legislation that specifically targets simulations of serious crimes against persons, particularly those involving children or extreme violence. Clear legal standards can prevent overreach while protecting society from the most harmful content.

Conclusion

The rapid advancement of virtual reality technology demands that our legal frameworks evolve to address new forms of potential harm. Criminalizing VR simulations that depict child sexual abuse, torture, and similar extreme content represents a necessary and proportionate response to protect vulnerable individuals and maintain societal standards of human dignity. The immersive nature of VR, the risk of escalation to real-world crimes, and the need to protect children from exploitation all support taking decisive legal action.

As we shape the digital future, we must ensure that technological progress does not come at the expense of fundamental human values. Prohibiting the most harmful forms of VR content sends a clear message that some boundaries remain inviolable, even in virtual spaces. The cost to free expression is minimal compared to the potential benefits of preventing the normalization of heinous crimes and protecting those who cannot protect themselves.

Introduction

The rapid advancement of virtual reality (VR) technology has opened new frontiers in entertainment, education, and social interaction. One of the most compelling reasons to criminalize harmful VR simulations is their potential to cause real psychological and emotional damage. While some may dismiss virtual crimes as "harmless fantasy," research in psychology and neuroscience demonstrates that immersive experiences—especially those involving violence, exploitation, or trauma—can have lasting effects on the human mind.

1. Desensitization and Normalization of Harmful Behavior

Studies on media violence have long established that repeated exposure to graphic or exploitative content can desensitize individuals, making them more tolerant of real-world abuse (Anderson et al., 2010). VR takes this effect to an extreme by placing the user inside the scenario, creating a heightened sense of presence and emotional engagement. This desensitization does not remain confined to the virtual world; it can spill over into real-life attitudes, increasing the risk of actual criminal behavior.

2. The Trauma of Victimization in VR

While VR simulations of abuse may not involve physical harm, they can still inflict profound psychological trauma—particularly when the victim is a real person whose likeness or identity is used without consent. For example, deepfake technology combined with VR could allow perpetrators to create hyper-realistic simulations of non-consensual acts involving real individuals, subjecting them to digital abuse that feels indistinguishable from reality. The emotional distress caused by such violations is no less real than if the abuse had occurred in person. Criminalizing these acts would send a clear message that digital exploitation is just as unacceptable as its physical counterpart.

3. The Exploitation of Vulnerable Populations

VR simulations of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) present an especially egregious threat. Even if no real children are harmed in the production of such content, the mere existence of these simulations fuels demand for real-world exploitation. The dark web has already demonstrated how digital abuse material—even when fictional—can normalize and encourage real crimes. By criminalizing VR CSAM, law enforcement can disrupt the pipeline that leads from virtual depravity to actual child abuse.

The Legal and Ethical Justification for Prohibition

Beyond psychological harm, there are strong legal and ethical arguments for treating harmful VR simulations as criminal offenses.

1. The Doctrine of "Harmful Speech" and Virtual Harm

Many legal systems already recognize that certain forms of speech—even if not directly causing physical injury—can constitute actionable harm. Hate speech, incitement to violence, and revenge porn are all examples of content that, while not physically destructive, inflict significant social and psychological damage. VR simulations of illegal acts fall into this category. 2. The Precedent of Existing Laws Against Digital Abuse

  • The U.S. PROTECT Act expands penalties for child exploitation, including digital forms.
  • Japan’s revised Penal Code criminalizes the distribution of deepfake pornography, recognizing its severe harm.

If harmful VR simulations are permitted, they risk becoming mainstream, particularly as VR technology becomes more accessible. What begins as niche "extreme content" could gradually seep into broader entertainment, desensitizing entire populations to violence and exploitation. History shows that once society normalizes certain behaviors—such as public flogging or animal cruelty—it becomes harder to reverse course.
